# Dallas Cowboys' Indoor Practice Facility Collapses During Severe Thunderstorm; Multiple Injuries Reported

**By CNN Staff**

IRVING, Texas — The roof of the Dallas Cowboys' indoor practice facility collapsed Saturday afternoon as a powerful thunderstorm swept through the region, injuring at least a dozen people who were inside at the time, according to emergency officials.

The structure, a large domed practice bubble, buckled under high winds shortly after 3 p.m. local time as a line of severe storms moved across the area, bringing wind gusts that meteorologists estimated exceeded 60 to 70 miles per hour.

## Injuries and Emergency Response

Emergency crews responded within minutes of the collapse. At least 12 people were transported to area hospitals, officials said, with injuries ranging from minor to serious. One individual sustained a spinal injury and was reported to be in critical but stable condition.

"We were able to account for everyone inside the facility," a spokesperson for the local fire department said during a press briefing. "Given the scale of the structural failure, we are fortunate the outcome was not far worse."

Rescue workers combed through the twisted metal framing and collapsed fabric roofing in search of anyone who might have remained trapped, but authorities later confirmed all occupants had been located.

## Eyewitness Accounts

Witnesses described a terrifying scene as the storm intensified and the structure gave way.

"It happened so fast," said one staff member who was near the entrance. "The wind picked up, the walls started shaking, and then the whole thing just came down on top of us. People were yelling and running for the exits."

Another eyewitness recalled the sound of the collapse. "It was like a giant crack, and then everything went dark. You could see daylight coming through where the roof used to be. Guys were helping each other get out from under the debris."

Members of the team's staff and rookies participating in offseason activities were reportedly among those present when the roof failed.

## Investigation Underway

Officials said an investigation would be launched to determine whether the structure met building and weather-safety standards. Questions were expected to focus on how the facility withstood the storm's wind load and whether the design was adequate for severe weather conditions common to the region.

The Dallas Cowboys organization released a brief statement expressing concern for those injured. "Our thoughts are with everyone affected. We are cooperating fully with emergency personnel and are grateful for their swift response."

The National Weather Service had issued severe thunderstorm warnings for the area shortly before the collapse.

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

---

*Note: This article is written in a general CNN-style news format. For factual reporting on any real event, please consult verified news sources.*

**IRVING, Texas** — The Dallas Cowboys' indoor practice facility collapsed Saturday afternoon during a severe thunderstorm, injuring at least a dozen people, including a scouting assistant who suffered a spinal injury that would leave him paralyzed.

The metal-framed, fabric-covered structure buckled and caved in around noon as roughly 70 players, coaches, staff members, and media personnel were inside during a rookie mini-camp workout. High winds, estimated by the National Weather Service to have gusted near 60 to 70 miles per hour, struck the facility as a line of storms rolled through the area.

## Scene of Chaos

Witnesses described a sudden, terrifying failure of the structure. The facility's steel supports gave way and the roof collapsed inward, trapping several people beneath twisted metal and torn fabric.

Special teams coach Joe DeCamillis and scouting assistant Rich Behm were among the most seriously hurt. Behm, 33, suffered a fractured spine and was paralyzed from the waist down. DeCamillis sustained fractured vertebrae in his neck.

## A Photographer's Account

Dallas Cowboys team photographer was among those present and later recounted the harrowing moments. Photographers on the scene described watching the walls shudder before the roof came down, sending people scrambling for the exits and diving for cover.

"It happened so fast," one photographer present recalled. "The wind hit and the whole thing just came down on top of us. You could hear the metal groaning and then it collapsed. People were shouting, trying to get others out from under the debris."

Images captured in the aftermath showed the flattened structure, its framework crumpled and the protective covering shredded and draped over the wreckage.

## Emergency Response

Emergency crews from Irving Fire-Rescue responded quickly to the scene, treating the injured and transporting several to area hospitals.

"We had a partial to full collapse of the structure," an Irving Fire Department spokesman said at the scene. "Our crews worked to account for everyone inside and to extricate those who were trapped. Given the scale of the collapse, we're fortunate the injuries were not more severe."

Officials confirmed that all individuals inside the facility were accounted for and that the most critically injured were promptly hospitalized.

## Jones Responds

Team owner Jerry Jones expressed relief that the incident had not resulted in fatalities and concern for those injured.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone who was hurt today, especially Rich Behm and Joe DeCamillis and their families," Jones said. "This is a very difficult day for our organization. We're thankful that it wasn't worse, but our focus right now is entirely on the people who were injured and making sure they receive the best possible care."

Jones added that the organization would cooperate fully with investigators to determine the cause of the collapse.

## Questions Over the Structure

The facility, built in 2003 by a manufacturer of fabric-covered structures, immediately drew scrutiny from engineers and safety officials regarding whether it was adequately designed to withstand high winds. The collapse prompted renewed questions about building standards for such structures.

Federal weather officials noted the storm's intensity but stopped short of attributing the collapse solely to the weather, leaving the door open for a broader engineering review.

The incident stood as a sobering reminder of the vulnerability of large temporary and semi-permanent structures to severe weather — and, for the Cowboys organization, marked one of its most difficult days off the field.
